At the monthly meeting of the women's self-help group in Rampura, Alka, the treasurer, had accused Jasleen in front of everyone: "You lost the dairy receipts again. How can we trust you with anything?" Jasleen went red, and she said nothing. Two days later Alka found the receipts folded inside her own ledger.
That evening she walked to Jasleen's house, past the flour mill, and stood in the courtyard. "I blamed you in front of all twenty women, and I was wrong. The receipts were in my ledger. I'm sorry. No excuse."
Jasleen kept sorting spinach. "Everyone looked at me like a thief."
"I know. What would help?"
"Say it at the next meeting. The same way you said the first thing."
At the next meeting Alka stood up, her voice steady, and said it plainly. She also started a receipt register that two members sign every week. Jasleen sat beside her when it was passed round.

qa.q: Where did Alka find the dairy receipts?
qa.a: Folded inside her own ledger.

qa.q: What did Jasleen feel after being blamed at the meeting?
qa.a: Jasleen felt humiliated and wronged, saying that everyone looked at her like a thief.

qa.q: Which part of Alka's repair made it one Jasleen could feel?
qa.a: Apologising without excuses, asking what would help, then correcting it in front of the same twenty women and starting a signed receipt register so it wouldn't happen again.

qa.q: How might the other women see Alka after she stands up to correct herself?
qa.a: They would likely trust her more as treasurer, seeing someone who owns mistakes openly, and would stop seeing Jasleen as careless.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who wrongly blamed someone in public and repairs it by naming the mistake, apologising plainly, asking what would help and changing the system.

Dear Diary,
Today Ammi asked again if I'd go up and help Maria with her reading at six. I said, "Yes, Ammi, of course!" in my best voice. Then at six I suddenly had to sort my stickers. And have a long bath. By the time I came out it was seven, and Maria's mother had gone back upstairs.
That's the fourth time this week. Ammi thinks I'm just forgetful.
Truth is, I don't want to. Maria is six and she cries when she gets a word wrong, and it takes up all my cartoon time. But when Ammi asks, her face is so hopeful that "no" gets stuck. So "yes" comes out, and then my feet just go somewhere else.
Maybe tomorrow I'll forget again.
Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do at six instead of helping Maria?
qa.a: Sorted stickers and had a long bath.

qa.q: Why does "no" get stuck for Dilnaz?
qa.a: Ammi's face looks so hopeful that refusing feels impossible, so Dilnaz agrees cheerfully and then resists by "forgetting".

qa.q: What could Dilnaz try instead of forgetting again?
qa.a: Telling Ammi honestly that the sessions are hard and take all the cartoon time, and maybe offering two evenings a week instead of every day.

qa.q: What might Maria's mother think after going back upstairs four times?
qa.a: She may feel let down and puzzled, thinking Dilnaz is unreliable, without knowing Dilnaz never really wanted to say yes.

grounding: Shows a child who cheerfully agrees to an unwanted job and then keeps forgetting, because saying no directly feels impossible.

In their village near Thrissur, Umma and Elizabeth aunty from next door ran a small tea shop by the bus stop. Every afternoon Umma asked, "Salma, wash the glasses after school, okay?" and Salma, nine, said, "Yes, Umma! Of course!" with a big smile.
Every afternoon she then forgot. She went to see the ducks on the canal, or started a very long game of hopscotch. When she came back, the glasses were already shining on the rack.
On Friday Elizabeth aunty caught her arm, gently. "Salma, you say yes every day. And every day you disappear. Is there something about the glasses?"
Salma twisted her plait. "The soap smells horrible. It stays on my hands all evening. But Umma is so tired, I can't say no."
Elizabeth aunty laughed softly. "Then say that. We'll find you another job."

qa.q: Where did Salma go instead of washing the glasses?
qa.a: To see the ducks on the canal, or to start a very long game of hopscotch.

qa.q: Why did Salma keep saying "Yes, Umma!" if she didn't want to wash the glasses?
qa.a: Umma looked so tired that saying no felt wrong, so Salma agreed cheerfully and then resisted by disappearing instead.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth aunty's question make possible?
qa.a: It gave Salma a safe chance to say the real reason, the soap smell, so the job can be swapped instead of the forgetting going on 🙂

qa.q: How might Umma see the shining glasses on the rack each day?
qa.a: Umma may think Salma simply forgets, and perhaps feel tired or let down, not knowing Salma hates the soap but can't say so.

grounding: Illustrates a child who says yes brightly to a chore and then always slips away, her resistance coming out sideways because a direct no feels impossible.

Since Papa made the new rule, that Eshaan must help at the hardware shop in Chhindwara every Sunday instead of playing cricket, Eshaan, fourteen, had not argued once.
He came at nine sharp. He stood behind the counter with his jaw set. When Papa asked him to sort the screws by size, he picked them up one at a time, turned each over, and dropped it into the tin as if it weighed a kilo. A twenty-minute job took two hours. "Everything okay?" Papa asked.
"Hmm."

Looking back at my first year, the notes were the worst part. My cousin Mahima and I shared a small flat near college, and I was, I admit, not a great dishwasher. But I didn't know she minded until the notes started. "Congratulations on washing ONE spoon! A historic day." Then: "The sink would like to meet you sometime. It's heard so much about you."
I felt ambushed every time I walked into the kitchen. You can't argue with a sticky note. I started coming home late just to avoid them.
Then one evening, instead of writing back something nasty, which I'd already drafted, I knocked on her door. "Mahima, I'm getting the notes. I think you're really fed up. What exactly do you want me to change?"
She went quiet, then said, "Wash up the same night. That's it." We made a rota on an actual piece of paper. Now she calls me "Deepak the Dishwasher", but to my face, and I laugh.

qa.a: "The sink would like to meet you sometime. It's heard so much about you."

qa.q: What turning point ended the notes?

passage:
I'm Kalyani, and I head the science department at a school in Kolkata. In June I proposed moving Class 9 practicals to a new project-based format. Everyone agreed, Arnab included. "Sounds good," he said, nodding.
By August his section hadn't started. The planning sheet was blank. The rubric he'd promised by the 15th never came. Each time I asked, he smiled: "Almost there."
I don't know what was going on in his head. But it slowly struck me that I had never heard him say what he actually thought of the plan. In that June meeting, three senior teachers had spoken warmly for it first. Maybe "sounds good" was the only answer that felt available.
So I stopped chasing the rubric. Over tea I said, "Arnab, I may have rushed that meeting. If you think this format is wrong for your section, I really want to hear it. You won't be in trouble."
He put down his cup. "Honestly? I think it'll eat all the revision time."

qa.q: What did Arnab say each time Kalyani asked about the rubric?
qa.a: "Almost there."

qa.q: What did Kalyani come to believe about Arnab's "sounds good"?
qa.a: Kalyani suspected Arnab disagreed but didn't feel able to say so after three senior teachers had praised the plan, so the objection showed up as delay.

qa.q: Which choice by Kalyani opened the real conversation?
qa.a: Dropping the chasing, admitting the meeting may have been rushed, and saying Arnab could disagree without trouble, which let him name his worry about revision time.

qa.q: What might the June meeting have felt like for Arnab?
qa.a: With senior teachers already praising the plan, Arnab may have felt that disagreeing would look difficult or disloyal, so agreeing seemed safer.

grounding: Shows a department head who sees a teacher agree to a plan and then miss every milestone, realises the disagreement was never voiced, and makes it safe to say no.

Project coordinator's note, Vandana, Wednesday
For a week Madhuri's messages have had an edge. "Sure, whatever works for YOU." "Noted. As always." In Monday's call she said, "Great, another change, love that," with a smile that didn't match. She's still doing all her work, on time. But something's off.
I could have ignored it or answered the tone. Instead, after today's call I asked her to stay back for two minutes.
I said, "Madhuri, I think I've missed something here. I'd rather hear it straight from you than guess. Is something I've done bothering you?"
She hesitated, then it came out: I had moved her client presentation to Friday without asking, twice, and she'd had to cancel taking her mother to a hospital appointment. "I didn't want to seem difficult."
I apologised, and we agreed: no schedule changes without asking her first. She laughed, properly this time. "Thank you for asking."
Next: check with the rest of the team about schedule changes.

qa.q: What had Vandana done twice without asking?
qa.a: Moved Madhuri's client presentation to Friday.

qa.q: Why had Madhuri's irritation come out in edged messages instead of plain words?
qa.a: Madhuri didn't want to seem difficult, so the anger about the schedule changes leaked out sideways in sarcastic lines.

qa.q: What did Vandana's words "I think I've missed something here" do well?
qa.a: They took responsibility gently and made a straight answer safe, so Madhuri could name the real problem and they could agree on a fix.

qa.q: What would change if Vandana had snapped back at the tone?
qa.a: Madhuri would likely have become more guarded, the schedule problem would have stayed hidden, and the edge in the messages would probably have grown.

grounding: Shows an adult who senses a colleague's veiled irritation, says gently that something may have been missed, and welcomes a direct answer, which ends the sarcasm.

Jaya's been prickly all week. "Oh, don't get up, I'll do the groceries again, it's my hobby." Tonight, when I said I'd be late on Saturday, she said, "Of course. Your schedule is the important one." Then she smiled and went to her room.
My first instinct was to be prickly back. Instead I knocked. I said, "Jaya, I think I've missed something, and I'd really rather you just told me. I won't get defensive." (I tried very hard not to.)

Fair. Completely fair. We made a list on the back of a receipt, and I'm doing Saturday's shopping before I go out.

"Sumit, your mother tells me you're the loudest boy in your class and a mouse at the dinner table. Let your Mridul chacha tell you something.
At fifteen, in Allahabad, I was two people. At school I was cricket captain, cracked jokes at the back, argued with umpires. At home, in front of my grandfather, I said 'ji' and nothing else. I never brought a friend home. I never told the family about matches. It kept the peace: nobody at home scolded my loudness, and nobody at school saw me go quiet.
Then I won the inter-school trophy. Every other boy's family was in the stands. Mine didn't know the final was happening. And my friends didn't even know I had a grandfather.
I'd kept the rooms so separate, beta, that nobody on either side really knew me.
Your school's sports day is next month. Maybe tell your Papa."

qa.a: "Ji" and nothing else.

qa.q: Why did keeping school and home separate feel sensible to young Mridul?
qa.a: It kept the peace: nobody at home scolded his loudness and nobody at school saw him go quiet, so each world stayed easier to manage.

qa.q: What choice is Mridul chacha nudging Sumit toward?
qa.a: Letting the two worlds meet a little, like telling Papa about sports day, so the family can see the confident side too.

The rain came down so hard that Hrithik's cycle chain snapped right outside Tejas's building, and there was nowhere else to go. Tejas, sixteen, hesitated at the door. Nobody from school had ever been inside.
At school Tejas was the loudest voice in drama club, the one who argued with the director and did impressions of the principal. Here, the moment Papa looked up from the newspaper, Tejas's shoulders dropped. "Ji, Papa. My friend. Only till the rain stops." Wednesday, 1 am
Minakshi Masi died on Monday. Exams start tomorrow. Mummy said on the phone, "Stay, write your papers. Masi would scold you if you came." So I stayed.
I've done something strange. I've put it all in a box in my head. When I think of her laugh, I say, not now, and go back to thermodynamics. It works. I studied nine hours today. Priya thinks I'm being very brave. I don't know if it's brave. It's just a lid.
But I've promised myself the box gets opened. On the 18th, after the last paper, I'm taking the night bus home. I'll sit in Masi's room with her sewing tin and her old radio and cry as much as I need. I've told Mummy. She said she'll be there.
Until then: lid on. Revise chapter 4.

In Nagaur, Sachin was the agriculture officer everyone liked. On Tuesday Kashish walked past the panchayat hall and saw him with a group of farmers: crouched beside an old man, explaining the new seed scheme for the third time, laughing at a joke about goats, never once looking at his watch.
That evening he came home at eight. Kashish had kept his favourite bajra roti warm. "How was the day?" "Fine." "The seed meeting?" "Kashish, please, not now." He ate facing the TV and went to bed.
She lay awake. She had seen the patience and the laugh. They weren't gone; they just seemed used up before he reached their door.
On Sunday she said, gently, "The farmers get your best hours. Could we have one of them? Maybe Sunday morning, a walk to the lake, before your phone starts?"
Sachin was quiet, then nodded. "I didn't realise there was nothing left by the time I got home."

qa.q: What had Kashish kept warm for Sachin?
qa.a: His favourite bajra roti.

qa.q: What did Kashish realise as she lay awake?
qa.a: That Sachin's patience and laughter weren't gone, just used up on the farmers before he reached home.

qa.q: What did Kashish's Sunday request get right?
qa.a: It named the pattern without blame and asked for one protected time, a Sunday walk before the phone starts, when Sachin still has energy.

qa.q: How might the farmers see Sachin, compared with how Kashish sees him at home?
qa.a: The farmers see a patient, cheerful officer who never checks his watch, while Kashish mostly meets a tired, curt man who comes home at eight.

grounding: Illustrates a wife who notices her husband is warm and patient with farmers but curt and drained at home, and asks for time before his energy is spent.

passage:
Noor: are you free? i'm in the office bathroom
Thomas: what happened?
Noor: two things at once. the bank called about the card during the client review. third call this month
Noor: and while i was declining it, Sam texted "we need to talk tonight"
Noor: i've kept these apart for months. work doesn't know about the money, Sam doesn't know about the money, nobody at work knows about Sam
Noor: today they all hit at the same time and i walked out mid-presentation
Thomas: ok. breathe. you're not in trouble with me
Thomas: those walls kept you going. but that's a lot to carry alone
Noor: i know
Thomas: can you tell your manager you need twenty minutes? then tonight, one thing at a time
Thomas: and for the card, maybe book a session with a proper debt counsellor this week. i'll sit with you when you call
Noor: ok. yes. thank you

qa.q: What did Sam text during the client review?
qa.a: "We need to talk tonight."

qa.q: Why did Noor walk out mid-presentation?
qa.a: The worries Noor had kept sealed apart, the money and Sam, pressed in at the same moment, and the walls that usually made work possible gave way.

qa.q: What steps does Thomas suggest to get through this?
qa.a: Asking the manager for twenty minutes, handling one thing at a time tonight, and booking a debt counsellor this week with Thomas there for the call.

qa.q: How might Noor's colleagues have seen the walk-out?
qa.a: Knowing nothing about the money or Sam, colleagues would likely be puzzled or worried, since Noor usually seems to have everything under control.

grounding: Shows an adult who has kept a money problem and a relationship problem walled off from each other and from work, until both press at once and the walls crack.

passage:
Jaya ran the small grocery shop at the Bundi bus stand like clockwork: accounts neat, customers greeted by name, jokes for the schoolchildren buying toffees. Nobody would have guessed at the two locked rooms she carried.
In one: the wholesaler's bill, three months unpaid, which she had never mentioned to anyone. In the other: Gautam, her husband, who wanted to move to Jaipur for work, and the quiet fights they'd been having every night. She never spoke of Gautam at the shop, or of the bill at home.
On Thursday both doors opened at once. The wholesaler's man arrived asking loudly for payment, just as Gautam walked in to argue about Jaipur. Customers turned. Jaya's hands shook so badly she dropped a jar of pickle on the floor.
That night she told Gautam everything about the bill. He was silent for a long time. Then he said, "Tomorrow we go to the cooperative bank together and ask for proper advice. After that, we talk about Jaipur."

qa.q: What did Jaya drop when both problems arrived at once?
qa.a: A jar of pickle.

qa.q: Why had keeping the bill and the fights in separate rooms felt useful to Jaya?
qa.a: It let her run the shop smoothly and stay cheerful with customers, instead of being swamped by both worries at once.

qa.q: What turning point came after the walls cracked?
qa.a: Telling Gautam everything about the bill that night, which led to a plan to go to the cooperative bank together for proper advice and then talk about Jaipur.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt learning about the three-month-old bill?
qa.a: Gautam was probably shocked and hurt at being kept out, but his calm plan for the next day shows he wanted to face it together.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who keeps a debt away from her marriage and her marriage away from her shop, until both burst in at once and she chooses to share them.
